outcomes.absoluteFailure:
In certain towns of Eriador, travellers' stories describe great black wolves bred by Orc captains as mounts for war. These animals are said to descend from strains of wolves selected over generations for their strength and their docility towards their masters. Merchants recount that the Orcs feed and train them in vast caverns, where they learn to recognise the weapons, armour, and commands of their riders. The mightiest Wargs serve as mounts for chieftains, while the others accompany raiding convoys and guard the mountain passes. Their reputation as malevolent creatures would chiefly arise from the violence committed by the warriors they carry.

The stories circulating in inns also maintain that these beasts cannot enter a fortified town unless led by an Orcish master. The walls, massive gates, and noise of the streets would disorient them, since their training accustoms them to open spaces and mountain tracks. Some travellers claim that the ringing of great bells is enough to drive them back, while others ascribe this protection to the fires kept burning upon the ramparts. Townsfolk familiar with these traditions believe that a settlement whose gates are guarded remains safe from Wargs even when the neighbouring roads are threatened. The real difficulty, then, would be to prevent their Orcish riders from approaching the fortifications.
outcomes.failure:
Merchants' and soldiers' accounts describe Wargs as great wolves employed by Orcs to range the roads and pursue travellers. Their size, speed, and endurance make them useful to armed bands seeking to surprise a convoy or hunt down fugitives. Witnesses report that they can follow a trail over long distances and recognise passages habitually used by Men. Some are strong enough to carry a rider, while others accompany warriors on foot. Townsfolk know these creatures chiefly through the warnings brought by travellers arriving from the mountains or from less secure borderlands.

An explanation widespread among guards and caravaners attributes their concerted movements to the military organisation of the Orcs. Wargs are said to be trained to answer calls and recognise signals from their riders. Their howls would transmit these commands from one group to another, like the horn-calls used by soldiers. Escorting troops' accounts stress the importance of Orcish leaders, whose loss would throw the packs into disorder. Some men-at-arms therefore regard Wargs principally as an auxiliary force, formidable when directed but unable to plan an attack on a well-protected convoy by themselves.
outcomes.partialSuccess:
The traditions of Eriador's towns identify Wargs as great malevolent wolves associated with Orcs and the wild lands. Caravans' accounts describe them as swift and powerful creatures, able to pursue travellers over long distances. Some carry Orc warriors, while others accompany armed bands on raids. Their keen sense of smell and acute hearing enable them to recover a trail and detect the movements of Men. The best-known accounts also speak of their gatherings in packs and of the howls they exchange as they travel.

You know that Wargs possess an intelligence greater than that of ordinary animals and that they communicate in a language of their own. They can act in concert, choose their movements, and pursue purposes without waiting for a rider's orders. Merchants' tales emphasise their ability to discover the roads taken by convoys and follow travellers who leave the main routes. Garrison troops and escorts know of their alliance with Orcs, but accounts also tell of encounters with solitary packs. Their presence therefore poses a danger to travel between human settlements independently of the movements of Orc-bands.
outcomes.success:
The towns of Eriador preserve many accounts of Wargs, handed down by merchants, soldiers, and travellers who journey along the ancient roads. These testimonies describe creatures capable of understanding the movements of Men and organising their actions with others of their kind. Wargs possess their own language, through which they exchange warnings, gather a pack, and prepare an attack. Their association with Orcs rests upon an ancient alliance, yet they retain their own organisation and can pursue independent enterprises. Some serve as mounts, while others join raids as scouts and pursuers.

Caravaners' accounts stress their ability to exploit the constraints imposed by roads. A convoy progressing through a narrow pass, crossing a ford, or traversing woodland has different possibilities of movement from a group travelling across open ground. Wargs can recognise these differences and alter their movements to reach a favourable passage. A pack may follow travellers from a distance, disperse along several paths, or attempt to isolate men who stray from the group. The howls exchanged by its members allow them to remain in contact and coordinate their movements even when vegetation or relief separates them.

Those charged with keeping the roads safe also know that Wargs are independent. The disappearance of an Orc-band or the death of its riders leaves packs still capable of acting alone. Travellers may therefore report Wargs in a region where no gathering of Orcs has been seen. Urban traditions place great importance upon comparing accounts: attacks in several places may result from the movements of a single group, but corroborating testimony is needed to recognise the nature and extent of the threat.
outcomes.absoluteSuccess:
The deepest knowledge possessed by the townspeople of Eriador brings together the memory of the roads, military testimony, and historical traditions preserved in the old centres of habitation. It distinguishes Wargs from natural wolves and from great animals used in war. Wargs possess an intelligence and a language that enable them to agree upon common actions, recognise their leaders, and prepare enterprises independent of those of the Orcs. Their alliance with the latter arises from shared interests and hostility towards the Free Peoples, but their organisation remains autonomous. Chronicles concerning unrest in the northern and eastern regions give particular attention to the wolf-like creatures that accompany the forces of the Shadow, while distinguishing direct observations from tales handed down from one generation to another.

The knowledge preserved by merchants and guards makes it possible to interpret the movements of Wargs across networks of roads and human settlements. A succession of reports about great wolves may reveal a wandering pack, while several attacks occurring close together may involve distinct groups or concerted movements. Wargs understand the constraints of the terrain and can recognise places where travellers slow down, scatter, or encounter obstacles. Their speed enables them to follow a convoy's movements and alter their approach in response to resistance. Experienced men know that their retreats may be calculated and that their howls are communications capable of coordinating several individuals.

The oldest traditions also speak of an origin connected with the corruption of living creatures by the powers of the Shadow. Learned people familiar with the tales of the Elves and Dúnedain distinguish Wargs from the Werewolves of the Elder Days, although popular stories sometimes confuse the two. Wargs remain corporeal beings whose physical abilities are those of great canids, yet their malevolent intelligence and organisation place them among the most formidable enemies of travellers. Urban records and accounts enable observers to connect their appearances with the movements of Orcs, while preserving the distinction between military alliance and the will of their own that governs the packs.

gmNote: GM verification: absolute failure — exclusively Orcish breeding and the supposed inability to approach towns; failure — the entire organisation is wrongly attributed to riders; successful results — merchants' traditions, the memory of routes, and Warg autonomy. The recording and comparison of testimony constitute a plausible cultural perspective, not a universally attested institution in every town of Eriador.
